According to 404 Media, the law enforcement forensics company Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass an iPhone security feature that automatically reboots the device after 72 hours of inactivity. Details below.

Background

About two years ago, Apple released the iOS 18.1 update, which introduced an "Inactivity Reboot" feature. If an iPhone remains unlocked for 72 consecutive hours, the system forces the device to reboot.

The core purpose of this feature is to make it harder for law enforcement and forensic tools to access data on a locked iPhone, because rebooting returns the device to a "Before First Unlock" (BFU) state, rather than remaining in the less restricted "After First Unlock" (AFU) state.

When an iPhone is in BFU state, some sensitive data remains protected by encryption keys; these keys only come into effect after the user first enters their passcode, at which point the device enters the AFU state.

Once in the AFU state, more device data can be accessed, until the iPhone reboots again and returns to BFU.

The iPhone's automatic reboot means that even if the device is seized by law enforcement, it may return to BFU state before investigators can access it, because obtaining a search warrant or transporting the device to a forensics lab both take time.

As 404 Media pointed out when iOS 18.1 launched, this feature also makes it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in AFU state for extended periods in order to develop or use intrusion methods.

GrayKey Reportedly Bypasses "Inactivity Reboot"

404 Media reported today that, according to a "training and tutorial video produced for law enforcement and dated early 2025," Magnet Forensics, the developer of the GrayKey phone unlocking tool, appears to have developed a method to bypass the iPhone's "Inactivity Reboot" feature.

The report states that Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve, and added an "Evidence Preservation Mode" to its existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are designed to maintain the iPhone's forensic state without immediately exposing the data stored on the device, allowing law enforcement to preserve that state while waiting for search authorisation.

The report notes that although the video does not detail the technical principles of the bypass mechanism, it explains that GrayKey can maintain the iPhone's AFU state even after the device reboots.

404 Media reached out to both Apple and Magnet Forensics for comment; neither responded to requests for comment. The outlet also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to manipulate the iPhone's clock, or to completely shut down the process responsible for expiring certain data.

Although the video appears to originate from early 2025, it remains unclear how long this technology has been available to law enforcement, whether it has been used in actual investigations, and whether it still works against the latest version of iOS.
